utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Today, Judge Harhoff being absent, Judge Mindua and I sit pursuant to the provisions of Rule 15 bis. Would you call the next witness, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honour. The next witness is protected witness 137.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And, Mr. Sachdeva, you may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness 137.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I just want to inform you, firstly, that the Court has granted you protective measures and therefore I will refer to you as Witness 137. And the first thing I want to do is I'm going to show you a piece of paper with your personal details on them and I would like you to confirm that for the Court. Are those details on that piece of paper correct and accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, they are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that it be tendered under seal, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P249, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness 137, I just want to ask you some question about your personal background.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, with your leave, may we go into private session for this part of the examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I also ask leave to lead the witness through these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you joined the KDZ, Witness 137, briefly describe to the Court your main role for that unit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Counter-sabotage protection as part of the police, practically had the same purpose and role as in peacetime, that is to detect, deactivate and disarm all lethal explosive devices. In wartime, we adopted our procedures accordingly, but the principle was the same. We were supposed to detect, disarm, and deactivate an explosive or make an analysis after an explosion of the fact conducive to confirming what had happened. Also at an enormous risk, we dismantled some of these device. Sometimes we extracted the charge from the devices and passed it on to the army for further use.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You said that you would also attempt to confirm what had happened in these incidents. What sort of -- what sort of roles did you play when you went to an incident, an on-site investigation, what sort of things did you look for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: At the time, it was generally believed that what we were doing was fruitless; however, we believe that if we examined documents and prove after a thorough analysis, each specific case of explosion, especially were it caused casualties and huge damage, that this proof will at some time in the future be of use to demonstrate the character of these actions and it proved to be true. Our KDZ team consisted of highly educated, electronic engineers, chemical engineers, military experts because Sarajevo was one of the military centres. And I think it is important to note that there were more Croats and Serbs than Muslims on this KDZ team.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness 137, just a small thing, we have limited time for examination, so I would ask you to confine your answers to my questions and if I require further information, I will ask you for that. Thanks for that. Now, I want to stick to shelling incidents. Did you conduct investigations into incidents from mortar fire within Sarajevo during your time at the KDZ?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, we conducted these on-site investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And with respect to the mortar incidents, was it your role to determine, firstly, the direction of fire of a mortar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes. That was the primary goal, to establish the direction of fire and to determine the angle of impact, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, actually you moved on to my next question. And with respect to the angle of impact, was that also your direct role in these investigations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes. Both mine and everybody else who was on the on-site investigation team, for a specific case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Was it also your role to identify the type of weapon or projectile that had been employed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you went to an on-site investigation, who else in your team would accompany you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: There were a few of us in the sense of enormous need for investigation because Sarajevo was impacted by more than a million shells. Sometimes there were two or three colleagues of mine with me, some other teams were composed in a different way because it was dictated by urgency of the specific situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, let's concentrate on the establishment of the direction of fire generally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before you do that, Witness, could you tell us, typically, who would those two or three other team members be and their qualifications?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, our team had very sophisticated expertise. We had all undergone training in recognising basic elements which are not basically difficult to grasp. And as I said, each team was set up by our boss who would send us to the ground for the investigation, from the people available at time at the KDZ. So at all times, teams were different because that's what the circumstances dictated, the circumstances of a specific on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, just take one particular on-site investigation as an example. I'd like you to tell me the qualifications and the training of those other two or three members. Just take any one that you went on with two or three other team members.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Specifically, when we did what was known at Markale II, I was some place on Tito Street near the national bank when I saw many cars with open boots and with dead -- and injured people inside. I immediately returned to the base because I realised that an on-site investigation would be pending. My boss told me to take a compass and with an another member of the team, who was a mechanical engineer, and there were also people from the security services centre in Sarajevo and others who participated in the investigation, and it was minutes for making decisions. That is how the two of us conducted this main investigation. At the same time, there were also UNPROFOR members who were interested in this investigation. There were from the French contingent and it lasted for about two hours, the analysis of the event, I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In that particular case, the other person from the bomb squad team was the mechanical engineer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness 137, just a quick question. You told us that you are an expert in chemistry. Did your qualifications render you competent and effective to undertake crater analysis of mortar incidents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: I believe that I and other KDZ members were even overqualified for these kind of things. During my university studies, I passed a few math exams that far exceed the need for these purposes; also physics, an another engineering subject as well that were far beyond the needs for analysis of the cases that we are discussing here. So we very quickly adopted our experience and expertise to the specific need after undergoing a very brief course for investigation. This has been demonstrated by the fact that none of our findings had been disputed because we never established or asserted anything unless we were completely sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can I take it from your answer, therefore, that the investigation into -- well, to conduct a crater analysis is a relatively uncomplicated process, is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: With certain theoretical introduction and study of showcases and the experience that we had in more than abundance, probably the best experience in the world in this particular area at the time, because as far as I know, in no war had the traces of shelling been so thoroughly analyzed as it was the case in this war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can you say roughly, during your time at the KDZ, how many mortar crater analyses did you conduct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Roughly speaking and from memory, I think a couple of hundred. Most of these analyses were made into official reports and some of them were just briefings that we did on a daily basis. After examining the craters, we just instinctively investigated the direction that they had come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So, generally, with respect to the direction of fire, briefly explain to the Court how you would go about conducting such an investigation. What sort of steps would you take in doing that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: If there are different fires, and different weapons in -- with mortar shells, it is very typical that if they hit a hard ground they leave a very clear and in most cases very clear trace which practically is an image of the angle, or rather, the azimuth of the shell and the impact angle of this shell. As a result of a very precise and sophisticated structure of the shell, its spreads explosion horizontally with regard to the trajectory and the longitudinal axis of the shell. That is how it has been structured in order to destroy as much lives as possible and the shrapnel is scattered around the impact place. So the first thing what we did was to find, if it was a mortar shell, to find the stabiliser, the fin, of the shell which will indicate which kind of type it was, whether it was 62, 120, or some other. Most cases we found a marking that it had been manufactured in Serbia. There's a KV marking on it which means Kraljevo in Serbia. Sometimes the fin was on the side but sometimes it penetrated the ground, depending on the type of the ground. And then we also collected as many as possibly of the rubble of the shell for further analysis. We secured the area around it in order to be able to carry out all the necessary measurements to establish the azimuth and, as precisely as possible, the impact angle of this grenade or shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you use the word "azimuth", do you mean the direction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, the direction from which the shell came.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So let's take the example where we have a mortar explosion on asphalt or hard surface. What kind of implements, or let's say instruments, would you use to determine the direction of fire, given that you would have mechanical traces on the ground?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: We used a military compass which is specifically designed for these purposes and we made good use of it. It has a cover with a mirror on it and a string down which you look. You aim it towards the direction that you estimate according to the shape of the trace from which the shell had come and after that, as precise adjustment as possible of the compass, we look at the azimuth angle and read it directly on the compass meter, clockwise, counting from the north.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now you mentioned earlier on in your testimony that you were involved in the investigation into the Markale II incident and I'm going to ask you specific questions about that incident and show you some photographs where you can explain the process of determining the direction of fire and the angle of descent. But before I get to that incident, I just want to ask you: What do you know about the accuracy of mortars, generally in -- when they were deployed in Sarajevo during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: It is common knowledge that in all armys that mortars are very precise, both in terms of direction and in depth, the direction of aiming and the depth, which means the specific location that you wish to hit. So those who studied mortars and who were in the army and those who fired shells, there's a saying that a mortar shell can be fired into the chimney of a house provided you wish to do. That means they are extremely precise. If they are probably used, if you use your sites properly on the mortar and take into consideration the elevation or the difference between the two points and if you use properly the tables, firing tables. So I am convinced that mortar fire is one of the most precise activities or operations conducted by artillery weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you say firing tables, just explain to the Court what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: That's practically a book containing very detailed tables. It's probably about two or three centimetres thick. And those who fire look parameters in these tables that they want to apply. They have all the information about the difference in height, what charge should be used and what the range with that charge can be achieved. So these are very sophisticated tables, very sophisticated for the use by those who fire mortars, in order to make them, I cannot say absolutely precise, but to be as precise as possible, that is technically possible and feasible to be accomplished by this mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If mortar positions are -- have remained there for one or two years, in other words, the base plates have been dug into the ground for one or two years, does that render the -- does that render the accuracy -- does it make a mortar more accurate or less accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: That makes it is more accurate. The crew gathers increasing experience being at a certain position and they have now had time to monitor the results of their firing for quite sometime.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: In such situations, is it possible to engage your target with only one round?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: If the crew has a great deal of experience, in that case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now let's move to the Markale II incident. Firstly, after the incident occurred, what time did you end up on the investigation site?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: It took perhaps less than ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And when you got to the investigation site, just describe briefly the scene that you saw there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: It was the last deepest circle of Dante's hell. Huge pools of blood, severed body parts, panic, fear, all of them civilians to the extent that I could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you got there, were you able to detect a crater that had been caused by the mortar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes. It was across a rail. It was relatively close to the pavement and there was a lot of blood all around it. It was along one lane of the road in front.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did that crater appear to you to have remained undisturbed? In other words, did the crater show any visible signs of tampering, when you got there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Given the large number of people who came to help carry the dead bodies away and the wounded, it was absolutely impossible for anyone to try and tamper with the crater, since dozens and dozens of people who were there would have spotted that attempt.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now I want to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to call up 65 ter 891 and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry, may I just examine the answer given to the last question. Do I understand you to say that because of the large number of people who were there to help to carry the dead bodies away, it was impossible for anyone to try and tamper with the crater. Or are you saying that because so many people were there, anyone who attempted or who did in fact tamper with the crater would have been detected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the way I see this, both your questions boil down to the same thing. The change -- any change to the crater would require heavy work. It would require work by hammers and by metal tools which would lead to a lot of banging sounds around the scene, which doubtless would have attracted a lot of attention. I didn't notice myself that anyone was trying to do anything like that and I very much doubt if anyone did. The crater was there up until perhaps two years ago. It remained intact for years and years after the actual shelling. Cars would drive over it without modifying the shape of the crater in any way. So the tracer -- the trace, the crater itself remained intact for years afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And did you say how -- how soon you got there after the impact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think about ten minutes later. The actual place is very close to the bomb squad HQ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, Witness 137, in the French translation, if I understood you correctly, you said that the shell that fell on Markale hit the ground next to a rail. Is that what you said, next to a rail? It's a track? Is that what it is, a railroad track, a rail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said road. One lane of the road. A lane of the road next to the pavement facing south, opposite the pavement -- there are tram tracks, that's true, but I haven't really mentioned them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. So the shell hit the sidewalk. It did not fall through the roof of the market or through some kind of wall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to set the record straight. It didn't fall on the pavement. It fell on one lane of the road running parallel to the pavement. It impacted against the road directly without hitting anything along its trajectory. Otherwise, there would have been some sort of damage to one of the roofs or one of the buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... if you have a shell, which instead of hitting the tarmac directly, hitting it direct -- directly a surface, would first fall through the roof of a building and then hit the ground. When you examine the impact on the ground, would it still be possible to determine with some accuracy the direction of the fire? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that is entirely impossible. The shell was built in such a way that it explodes at once. If a shell goes off in a treetop or it falls on a roof that's where the explosion occurs. It doesn't continue to travel from there. Once it explodes, once it hits an obstacle, it explodes, it goes into pieces and it stops being a shell, in the proper sense of the term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So unless there is a ricochet. Because we had an expert here who talked about bullets or shells that ricochetted. Isn't it possible to have ricochet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible. If we're talking about the -- a missile fired from a Howitzer or a gun, a delayed action projectile, it can go on ricochetting, hitting against other surfaces depending on the situation. But when have you a mortar shell, the important thing is the way it is built. The fuse is protected but when there is even the slightest amount of contact or impact, even if a shell hits as treetop, for example, that's where it ends up. That's where its trajectory ends. It stops being a single body. It fragments into shrapnel and it stops being a shell in the proper sense of the word. The way it is built is made to ensure this: Once it hits against something it goes into a thousand splinters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, I was going so show you a photograph, but I want to ask one or two questions following on from His Honour Judge Mindua's question to you. Firstly, do you -- in your work, did you ever experience working on weapons called modified air bombs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes. There was a period of time during which there was frequent activity using modified air bombs and yes, I did carry out on-site investigations in incidents involving modified air bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And with these modified air bombs, is it, as opposed to a mortar, is it possible to -- to have them ricochet off a surface before they eventually explode?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: The modified air bombs are makeshift projectiles. They are not standard issue weapons, in a manner of speaking. They were built on the spot improvised. They were makeshift weapons, homemade sometimes. This was an air bomb with a huge mass, a very massive weapon. Rocket motors were used. Those were taken from multiple rocket launchers, so this was a combination of a huge bomb that was used and the rocket motors that drove the bomb. Launching pads were used too. Charges were also produced that were not particularly aerodynamic, the symmetry of these charges or warheads were adjusted in a relatively simple way. Therefore, the weapons were no high-precision weapons. The general direction would normally be right, but as far as the -- the depth of the targeting was concerned, they were relatively imprecise in accurate weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you also in your work determine the direction from which modified air bombs came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Given the sort of marks that they normally left, given the sort of crater they would produce, it would be slightly difficult to determine the direction, unless of course it impacts against a vertical obstacle. For example, there is a very tall building at Alipasino Polje, near the Nedzarici student dormitory. There is still damage there caused by just such a bomb which shows clearly that the building was hit from a westerly direction, in this case, specifically, from the direction of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If you were able to determine the direction from which a modified air bomb came, and there were two opposing forces in relatively close proximity to each other in that particular area, would you be able to identify the particular force that fired that air bomb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The BH army had been disarmed before the war even began. All the weapons and equipment remained in the hands of what used to be the JNA. As for any Territorial Defence weapons, and those were substantial amounts of weapons as well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to use other factors than the -- the technical ones which relate to the firing of an air bomb. Don't use the knowledge that you have of who had weapons and who didn't have weapons. Would it be technically possible to say that the air bomb was fired by force A when force B was in relative close proximity to force A?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand your question correctly, Your Honour, I was in no position to actually establish that this was indeed fired, but I have heard witnesses say that these projectiles that were fired from Ilidza, their flight would normally be slow and they would normally be very noisy missiles. There were other people who saw these things fly through the air, the simple reason behind this being that they were not normally very slow missiles and they caused a lot of noise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sachdeva, what is the time estimate for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Four hours, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Four hours. Because I understand that it is essential that we finish his testimony today and I see no reason why we shouldn't. Of course a witness comes to give evidence in a trial like this. His testimony is important and that must be given consideration. But if we can accommodate the witness who has a particular need to travel then we will, as long as it is not inconsistent with the administration of justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I actually intend to finish hopefully in the first session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness 137, I just want to go back to my initial question on the air bombs and if you could just listen very carefully and answer it. His Honour Judge Mindua was talking to you about mortars and whether it was possible for a mortar to ricochet and then explode. In other words, not explode on first impact. And my question to you: With respect to modified air bombs, is it possible for a modified air bomb to not explode upon first impact, in other words, ricochet and then explode? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: I think with this sort of device it would be possible, depending on the angle of impact, when the actual fuse is not the first thing that is struck so it doesn't activate the projectile. That is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now I would like to bring up 65 ter 02 -- 02595 and these are photographs. And if we could go to the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness 137, do you see a photograph on your screen there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And do you recognise what's depicted in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes. I think this is Markale II.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And if we could move to page 5 of this exhibit, please. May that be zoomed up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: 137, do you see -- well, what do you see there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: I see the marks produced by the fall of a mortar shell, by the impact of a mortar shell. It did not fall under a 90-degree angle, that much is certain. And that affects the symmetry of the crater itself. So the angle of descent was further away from where I stood, towards the bicycles and the building right there next to the pavement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Just so we're clear, when you say you see an impact of a mortar shell, is this the mortar shell that landed or Markale, Mustafa Begovic Street on the 28th of August 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes. This is a 120-millimetre mortar shell, instantaneous. It's an artillery weapon and it's used to destroy manpower. It is built in such a way that it doesn't spray its deadly shrapnel all over symmetrically, but rather, in a horizontal fashion. The easiest way to explain this would be to liken it to the blades of a helicopter. Most of the shrapnel is sprayed within an area that is perpendicular to the axis of the shell itself, which is relatively low down, simply because the manpower which is usually targeted by a weapon like this is not high up but rather closer to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If -- well, from this photograph, are you able to make out the locations of north and south?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: South is from the centre of the crater, nearly perpendicular to the pavement and the building that you can see at the far end of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So the building is in the south. If you could just take a pen and put a S by the building, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, with this photograph of the crater, just take us through the steps that you took to determine the direction of fire. In other words, where did you use your compass and where did you determine the direction of fire from that crater, from the mechanical traces you see there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Just a small correction of the direction before I start with that, given the symmetry, because I can see the print, the impression of the impact. You can see that this is due south and once you get there, there's a shell landing at an angle that is not a 90-degree angle. We tried to establish which side it came from by using this indicator. Some of the shrapnel where the explosion is at its most powerful, which is the centre of the explosion itself, is sprayed over the ground in such a way that -- towards this area that I marked by this dotted line that's where the azimuth lay. So I would place this opposite the dotted line where I'm sitting now. I point my compass in that direction. It has a rope just like this pen, a very similar one, a string. And then I use my experience, with full respect for the symmetry of that side of the dotted line, and then I establish the direction in such a way. I do it by reading the angle from the compass that represents the azimuth. And in actual fact, this is the direction from which the shell arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Let's try and take this slowly. The spot that you have drawn beneath the dotted line, does that mark the centre of the explosion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: No. The centre of the explosion is the dot that I marked in red. That is the place where the shell actually landed. The centre of the explosion is at the point of balance within the shell, within the explosion itself. From that centre outwards the explosion -- the point of the greatest impact, the explosion spreads vertically in relation to the axis of the shell. It's like when you open an umbrella. So that's how the explosion spreads. The -- the spokes of an umbrella in relation to the handle. So that's how you discover this other marking, which is the dotted line. If you place that umbrella on the floor and suddenly opened it, it would lean in one direction and the canvas of the umbrella would touch the floor. This is a very rough analogy but it explains what I am talking about. This is the direction of the greatest impact because the explosion carries horizontally and in relation to the angle at which a shell landed it leaves an area which is the area that I marked by using this dotted line. This sort of symmetry is used for determining the azimuth which is the direction the shell came from, as well as the angle of descent of a given shell in relation to the main horizontal given, which is the ground itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you talk about the explosion spreading, on the photograph, do the mechanical traces illustrate the way the explosion spread and do you see more mechanical traces towards the south than you do towards the north?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: There were obvious mechanical traces, both in terms of the depth and their number between the point that I marked to the south, which means that to all practical intents, the shell came from the south, roughly speaking. The more precise definition of the direction from which the shell came is provided by the azimuth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Are you able to, with your pen, from the crater you see here to -- to draw the line that reflects the direction on this crater? In other words, to draw the azimuth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: The line that I have drawn is perpendicular to the dotted line that I had earlier marked. Therefore, this line would be the azimuth because it's 90 degrees with respect to this dotted line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, why couldn't it be said further to the right? I was asking why couldn't the direction be further to the right. I'm asking the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because when you analyse this kind of traces, you take the line of the most dense distribution of shrapnel or rather the traces of shrapnel on the asphalt that I marked with a dotted line. So this distribution of marks, which here is rather clear, indicates the basic direction which is marked by the dotted line, and at 90 degrees is the azimuth, which indicates the direction from which the shell came. Excuse me. Of course, when establishing the azimuth, we always take into account certain margin of error, which is plus/minus five degrees, because we cannot say with any 100 per cent certainty that that is the case because this is the statistical density and the total image left by the shell and of course you have to allow for certain subjective errors which is expressed in plus/minus five degrees. However, there were three or four of us on the team who established this direction. We made our individual notes and we compared the notes, and we coordinated approximately our findings. Afterwards, we heard that UNPROFOR had arrived at the same conclusion with regard to the direction that we had established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So it's absolutely important then to pinpoint the area with the most dense distribution of shrapnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And so I take it then if you are to go further to the right, locking at the screen, along the dotted line, you wouldn't start there, because the shrapnel distribution was not as dense as it was at the point that you have actually marked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we look at the distribution of shrapnel and we don't take their depth into account, then you can get a wrong picture. However, since the distribution of shrapnel where the depth is most -- the depth of the crater in the hard surface is greatest, it indicates 90 degrees and it leaves the strongest mark, not only the number of shrapnel pieces, but also their depth. When you look at this biggest depth on the pavement -- on the road, and I hope we shall look at some more pictures showing how technically the explosion is dispersed, this will show why we took this particular direction because it represents the deepest holes in the asphalt that I marked with the dotted line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So it's vitally important then that the scene not be disturbed before you do your investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. The investigation didn't last long. I cannot say whether it was an hour or two, but taking into consideration the importance of this event, we stayed longer, about one or two hours, but I know that a French artillery expert was there for about five to ten minutes. They measured all those parameters and then they left. However, we felt that our responsibility was greater in terms of providing and documenting this as best as possible and to remove any doubts or suspicions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What I meant was that if, for example, people had walked in the crater or had in some way managed to affect the distribution of shrapnel, then, of course, that would affect your identification of the area with the densest distribution of shrapnel, and you might very well be working from a wrong premise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to make a correction here between shrapnels and the holes made by them in a surface. We are not looking at shrapnel here. Perhaps there was not a single shrapnel piece and at that moment it's irrelevant. The hole caused by the shrapnel is such that it is ricochetted further on. We are talking about holes in the asphalt that can only be modified by hard hammering or by use of some heavy object which at the point was totally unimaginable. Even if you walk over this area, you wouldn't change or tamper anything in terms of the shape, the distribution and the depth of those most important craters for arriving at the facts that I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we understood how from the horizontal line, the dotted line which is the line that was made by shrapnel and you've made a perpendicular line which enabled you to establish the angle. Now my question is the following. If you can determine -- you have determined already the direction, which is very good. But can you tell us, do you know from what distance the mortar was fired. Is that possible, to establish the distance from what you've established here on this scene?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in response your question, I have to go back to the first part of your question in order to avoid any mistakes. We are not talking about shrapnel in this picture that exists there physically. There's no shrapnel there. There is the trace and the hole in the asphalt caused by the shrapnel impact and they flew away along with the piece of asphalt that they chipped, so you don't see shrapnel there. You can see just their impact. It's like an X-ray picture of a person, bones and things like that. So this is the image of how the shell fell, how the shrapnel was distributed and, as such, it speaks a lot about other basic information like azimuth and angle impact. The second part of your question concerning the source of fire, we did very exact measurements. And whenever we were not sure, we wouldn't claim anything. And I must say that about this particular angle of impact of the shell that we established here, there are a few combinations of firing parameters by mortars. It involves the difference in heights between two points, the number of charges, because a mortar shell has one, two, to six charges and the angle of firing. So based on these parameters that we had very precise in front of us, you cannot say exactly from which point the shell was fired, because there are several combinations of these parameters that would give us the same impact angle. However, we were encouraged when we heard on that day that there was a report saying that on that day there was no mortar activity from the positions of the BH army and therefore at that point we suspended our investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Witness, you are telling us that that particular day did you not establish or you couldn't conclude from what distance the shell was fired, but today, following some investigations, can you tell us if someone was able to establish from what distance this particular shell was fired? Do we know it today, in other words, following your investigations or did somebody find that out, that detail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Concerning the azimuth and even more importantly for the impact angle, there are several combinations. The mortar charge, the distance and the angle at which the shell was fired. So there's a series of possibilities indicating to the position from which the shell was fired. We -- that is why we cannot say precisely, yes, that was this location and no one can say that. Except, unfortunately, there was a radar that arrived to Sarajevo at the beginning of the war but it broke down very soon. It was intended to monitor and follow each projectile and based on the parabola, to identify the right position of firing. As far as I know, the French contingent provided this but allegedly it had already arrived malfunctioning in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'm not quite clear on this. I don't know who would be able to tell us, but as you know, this Trial Chamber will have to render a decision beyond a reasonable doubt. And with what you have told us and the evidence that you have presented, unless the Defence manages to show the contrary, but we could conclude that there is an incident that took place, that is obvious. But until now, you're telling us that no investigation was carried out, which would enable us to determine with precision the distance from which the shell was fired. And you are also not able -- you're not able to tell us who is responsible for it and, according to you and your experience, who could tell this Trial Chamber this so that this Trial Chamber can determine beyond a reasonable doubt who are the authors of this situation, who is espionage for this shelling.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are many military experts around the world in the most powerful and sophisticated army. These artillery experts could have their say in this case; however, my opinion is that, on the basis of the parameters that I have just shown you, neither of those experts would say be able to give you the precise location of the firing. There are, however, methods that we are not able to use and there are not at our disposal. Probably, had this radar been functioning at the time, it would have given us an almost 100 per cent accurate location. I understand your intention to look for solid evidence, but the only thing I can tell you is that on that day it has been established that the BH army had not been firing any mortars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Of course you and the members of your team, you live in Sarajevo, you have been there for years, you're familiar with the -- with the conflict and you're familiar with the locations where the forces are placed. Would that be true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't directly involved with the army. And therefore, I was not aware of the exact position -- and positions and demarcation lines. But roughly speaking, it was common knowledge that the slope of Mount Trebevic were occupied and at a rather low altitude from the foot, this leads to us a conclusion by analysing the impact angle, the layout of the buildings, et cetera is that this specific shell had come from the slopes of Trebevic. These were generally long-range shells.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And who occupied the slopes of Trebevic? Which forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serbian occupation forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So that's my question then, that all of this was common knowledge where the forces were placed. And the question that one must ask is to what extent that might have even subconsciously influenced the conclusions that you arrived at as to the direction from which the -- the mortar came.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that any unconscious influence in our reasoning was excluded. Although it was a deeply emotional moment, we looked death in the eyes on a daily basis because there's an estimate that over a million projectiles of various calibres landed in Sarajevo during the war. From our analysis, you can see that we were dealing only with exact things and we never made any claims if we were not sure, if we did not establish it as a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just one more question. You have drawn the direction from which this mortar came by drawing a line that's 90 degrees in relationship to the dotted line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the scientific basis for choosing 90 degrees as against, say, 135 degrees, or 150 degrees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there is some kind of confusion. I'm talking about this dotted line representing a characteristic line resulting from the angle of the impact of the shell and with respect to this line at 90 degrees, an azimuth is established. This azimuth is not 90 degrees. It's a different number shown by the compass. So the dystriomatical [as interpreted] drawing that you see here indicates how you arrive at the direction which is azimuth. Whether this line marked at 90 degrees is actually 90 degrees or some other figure is a completely different matter. The azimuth here, if I remember correctly, was 170. Had it been, for instance, 180, then these two sides would coincide and it will indicate a precise southerly direction. So it's ten degrees shorter of a straight line. So you have to make this distinction between the 90 degrees which is just a method of establishing the azimuth and the actual azimuth angle. These are two different parameters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But to be more practical, then, why couldn't that line which ends with the arrow be drawn somewhere between itself and the end of the dotted line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honours. I must say I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... if I could draw it myself. Just take a diagonal line between --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see this A here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I marked the azimuth with A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay, that's A. And let us say at the end of the dotted line to the right, that's C. If you had that marked C, why couldn't the azimuth be somewhere between --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean this one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Why couldn't the azimuth be somewhere between A and C, be midway between A and C?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. Have I put letter C at the place where you wanted me to put it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So the question is, why couldn't the azimuth be midway between A and C?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You asked me why this line cannot be between A and C. Is that your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your microphone was off and the witness didn't hear your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my microphone was off. You have put C at the place where I want you to put it. And the question I'm asking is, why couldn't the azimuth be placed between A and C, midway between A and C?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this is absolutely impossible because the trace left by the explosion on the ground clearly shows the angle under which the shell arrived as well as its direction. I think that this analogy can better be seen from drawings which are part of this file. They show how the grenade was designed. Hundreds of experiments had been made with these shells before the war in order to arrive at the best possible design, which means that its explosion spread as much as possible in this direction and produced as many shrapnel pieces as possible. I mentioned the analogy of the helicopter propeller and the most shrapnel spread radially with respect to the shell axis. Now I'm going to call it propeller and it will create the deepest impression on the ground. It would have to be the same as if the helicopter landed upwards, up side down on its propeller and dug itself into the ground. So the same happens with a shell. If this is the angle, this is where shrapnel go, they go upwards towards the windows of the buildings and on this side downwards, most shrapnel is where they go. There's a prominent line of big shrapnel holes where they were most powerful and fastest and this is what we call this dotted line and that's the rule. This is what the military theory says when these kinds of projectiles are being developed and it has been shown through mathematical formula and other methods. So this is common knowledge these are very exact data and unfortunately we see how they work in practice. This dotted line is the most important one. It is so clear in this -- in this picture and it's much more clear than in other cases because it indicates how the shell was tilted from the centre marked by this big dot, to the side from which it had come. And that's actually the azimuth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Well, yes. What I'm trying to get at it is the objective scientific basis on which you work, as distinct from what might be just an initial subjective assessment that is later confirmed by anecdotal evidence as to where particular forces were placed. But thank you. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just would like to assist the Trial Chamber by explaining that the Prosecution will be calling a mortar expert, Mr. Richard Higgs, who testified in the Galic case. And it is our submission that many of the questions that you, Mr. President and His Honour Judge Mindua have will be clarified at that stage. And I would also add that it's not the Prosecution's case and never has been that we will be able to determine the precise spot or the precise location of the mortar within a sphere of five to ten metres from where the shell was fired. However, our case is that it came from territory controlled by the VRS or the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps in a general direction and from a general area. It is not going to be possible to determine the precise location of -- for example, where a mortar round was located on the slopes of Mount Trebevic, if it is indeed proven that way. I would just add that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue. Well, we -- just one more question before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness 137, you have been clear but I just want to be -- just so that is assists the Trial Chamber. You said that this crater marked on the street here had remains up until about two years ago. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes. For several years it was there. Until two years a new asphalt layer was put two years ago, but there are other traces all around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So my question is, with respect to this crater, if, for example, a mortar -- an expert or an investigator had gone to this crater in 2002 and seen -- would that investigator see the same traces that we see here and would that investigator be able to determine, as you said, the 170 azimuth from those marks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Many traces of this kind were -- there was huge loss of life and when there was massacre were filled with red paint after the war. So they were literally filled with red paint and they stay there like red roses. After the end of the war, some of them were of course covered. After the paint had been poured into this shrapnel holes, I believe that all the other remaining parameters could probably roughly determine the direction of fire, but that was the moment when everything was most fresh and these were the clearest marks that would enable us to determine the direction which is immediately after the impact. However, this is -- was such a hard surface that it remained unchanged even with cars passing over it. It's a very solid asphalt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll take the break now. 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness 137, let's just stick with this photograph. Is the photograph still on the screen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Where you have drawn the A for the azimuth, can you just on top of the A write, because you have mentioned in your evidence, 170 degree, please. Just put the figure 170 there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now -- right. If I were to ask you to draw a line that goes in the direction of 220 degrees, would you be able to do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: [Marks]. 220?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yeah, that's right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: This is plus 50. Approximately like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, you said -- well, you've also indicated on the photograph that the margin of error in determining the direction of fire is plus or minus five degrees. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: In your experience, is it possible that from looking at this crater one can come to a determination that the direction of fire was 220 to 240 degrees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: I think the likelihood of that having been the correct angle is very low. I wasn't the only one who determined this angle. There was a colleague with me, a lot of people who were experienced in this sort of thing, and then we compared our results and this is the result that is based on most of the evaluations carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, who made the final decision? Whose responsibility was it to make the final decision as to the direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This report was signed by two persons, myself and another colleague of mine as well as the boss of our department, the bomb squad. There's three signatures, but despite these signatures, we kept on analysing this for a long time after. Having filtered all the information, the final decision is made by the boss, the head of our unit, and he is the one who signs the final assessment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The other colleague of yours who also signed, was he on the spot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness 137, just so that we're clear with the terminology, in your previous answer to my question, you stated that I wasn't the only one to determined this angle. And you speak about angle. I just want to be clear that we're talking about the angle that depicts the direction of fire and not the angle that represents the angle of descent; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Well, the way this is determined, who actually determines it and how we agree on it, that's in reference to both these angles. These are the two typical angles that one studies each time a shell falls. The first one is the azimuth, which is the position or the direction that the shell came from and the angle of descent, that is the angle at which it hit the ground. And what I mean is, both of these, we did both of these. We compared our results. We analysed our margins of error. So this is the result of a lot of discussion and the degree of certainty for this being accurate in terms of both the azimuth and the angle of descent is very, very high.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So just let me understand. The line which you have drawn there ending in A, with an arrow, represents both the direction of fire and the angle of descent.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: The line that ends with the letter A is the line showing the azimuth, or rather, the direction from which the shell came, the geographical direction, if you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Have you represented the angle of descent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can't see it in this diagram. Conditionally speaking, that would be this, the Alpha that I've just drawn. But that shows the angle at which the arrow, A, is to the building. However, it's difficult to show that by using this diagram. If we look at it from the side, from a lateral view, the image might be clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I just wanted to inform you that with respect to the angle of descent, I'm going to be showing the witness aids that would assist in that, assist for the Court to understand that. This is primarily related to the direction of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So, Witness 137, let's just confine ourselves at the moment to direction of fire. I want you to explain to the Court, using the mechanical traces that you see here in the photograph, why would it not be possible for this mortar to have come from a direction 220 degrees; in other words, from the direction that you have depicted with the vertical line going upwards to the south?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think at least the Prosecutor should explain to the Chamber why he is putting this figure of all figures to the witness, 220, since it's difficult for us to understand. I don't think it's easy for the Chamber to understand. Why 220 degrees? The witness himself never referred to that particular figure, did he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But I don't think it's for the Prosecutor to explain this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. But in the transcript there is a error; it's not 2230 but it's 220 degrees. And the question is why choose this 220 out of all angles?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As I was saying, I don't think it's for the Prosecutor to explain. If he does something which is meaningless then we can't make any sense of it. Is there a significance, Mr. Sachdeva, in the choice of 220?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, there indeed is a significance for that choice, and I can answer that, if you want me to. But perhaps...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, you must introduce it through evidence. But I don't wish to disturb the way you're presenting the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And that figure will be introduced through evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness 137, do you want me to repeat the question or do you remember what I asked you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, you asked why the line marked as A is not the S line, if memory serves. Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, I will. You have drawn there on the photograph 170, with the A, and that is your evidence from this crater of the direction of fire. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I asked you to draw or to identify direction of fire of 220 degrees and you have done that with a dotted line to the right, which is positioned to the right of the arrow with the A. Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So my question is this: Strictly sticking to the -- without marking the photograph for the moment, please, sticking to the mechanical traces that you see here on the photograph, I want you to explain to the Court why it is not possible that the direction of this mortar was 220 degrees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: I think the answer would be as follows. The geometry, the image, the imprint made by the shell against this horizontal surface, the tarmac, and the symmetry of that imprint as it were, of the impact, indicates the direction that I have just drawn which is the dotted line, the broken line, if you like, which shows a typical line of the maximum impact from the centre of the explosion spreading in a vertical direction in relation to the axis of the shell itself. The impression on the ground in terms of its depth and distribution shows the greatest certainty in relation to the direction of firing or rather --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, just so we're clear, you used the phrase "dotted line." Are you talking about the horizontal dotted line or the vertical dotted line pointing towards 220, just so we're clear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: I mean the line marked as C, the horizontal line marked as C.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well, okay. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: That is the reason why, by looking at this symmetry, we use symmetry when we slice an apple in half. We know exactly where we are going to slice it. And then we see the impression made by this shell in terms of the north/south direction and it can be clearly discerned what the angle of the shell was in relation to the centre, which is the thick dot that I drew where it hit against the ground, went off and then the concentration of dots, which is shrapnel, closer to the pavement. That's what it shows. The line leaning further to the left or further to the right is the average type of image, the average type of symmetry that occurs when you use a compass to mark this. And this is a widely -- universally, you might say, accepted method of taking this type of measurement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If you look at the -- if you look at the shrapnel marks in the area where you have drawn the dotted line that points to 220, in other words, to the -- on the right-hand side of this photograph, is there anything about the shrapnel marks there or the mechanical traces that enables you to say that the direction of fire is not 220 degrees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: There's a hint but a very vague one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand this correctly, the witness is being asked to confirm a negative fact. Back from where I come from, in my country, in our system, this would be referred to as a negative fact. Maybe it is just me finding it difficult to find my way around. How is this witness to confirm something that is a negative, to begin with?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me that he is simply asking him to say what are the -- the reasons for concluding that the direction of fire was not 220 degrees. I see nothing wrong with that. Yes, Witness, what are the reasons? What are the indicators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand the question, one of the reasons for me to rule out the 220 degree angle, is that the question? It's as follows. The previous image that I drew contains the following elements. What I marked. As to your question, we would need to have emphatic marks which I drew like this, roughly speaking. However, you can't see those on the ground. And that's why I put the question marks there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So I'm not sure I understood. What are the reasons for ruling out 220?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see these fields that I have drawn, the two elliptical shapes, and I put the question marks there to the left and to the right. There, I should be able to see marks that I did see at these other elliptical shapes that I'm about to mark additionally which was not the case. This is -- is an image that has now been multiply marked and it may be a bit unclear. Perhaps if we have another copy then I would be able to mark this more clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that feasible?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: We can -- sorry, Mr. President. I think we can get a clean image of the photograph and maybe the witness can explain it. Then, however, I would like to tender this -- tender this still. I'm wondering whether I could ask the witness to remove the question mark, elliptical diagrams and then they can then be marked on a separate, clean photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness 137, the elliptical image, shapes that you have drawn with the question marks, can you please erase them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Didn't he also mark something under the dotted lines? No, I'm asking whether he did not also just mark -- make a mark under the dotted line, whether that should not also be removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: No. As I understand it, that circle, that dot under the dotted line is the centre of the explosion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, that is not what I'm referring to. The -- the -- to the -- to the -- both to the left and right of the direction line. Under the dotted line, there are some marks there. Was that recently done?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Prosecutor. Because the ellipsis were filled in red. Maybe it would be better to have them empty again and just take out all the red that was in the ellipsis so that way we can still see the impact trace, the mechanical traces on the photograph itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes. I would be happy to ask the witness to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, those two elliptical shapes that you have drawn on the horizontal line marked C, can you erase -- can you erase it -- not the -- hold on, please. Hold on, please. I want you to erase the part that is inside the elliptical shapes; in other words, just the red -- the red part that obscures the mechanical traces but leave the circles, so to speak, as they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In other words, just go back to the dotted line alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: All right. If we can just go back to the dotted line.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And just one last thing on this photograph. Where you have drawn the dotted line that says towards 220, can you just put "220 degrees" on the top of that dotted line.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I would ask that that photograph be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P250, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can we now have a clean copy of this photograph on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness 137, on the previous photograph you drew two elliptical shapes with question marks. In your -- in your answer to explain why it was not 220 degrees, can you continue to do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Does he now have to redraw what was there before?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, I could ask the witness to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, you lead him in the way that you think is most appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Okay, Witness 137, just remember what we're trying to do here. I'm trying to ask to you use the traces that you see on the photograph and explain why the direction of fire is not 220 degrees. So, firstly, let's start by identifying again the centre of the explosion.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Then, with a dotted line, draw the direction of 220 degrees.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: In the previous image, I just marked 220 in a very approximate way. It should have been -- we should have added 30 plus 20 which makes 50 and here in the corner -- and well that doesn't matter, but I will show it anyway. This is 90 degrees and half of that would be 45, right? The previous direction, we know that to be 170. One should add a little more than these 45 here. There. I will show you. That would make it further to the right. That means this is a very rough sketch, but if we had something to measure the angle, we could have a more accurate representation of it. But roughly speaking, this would be further to the right. And what was your question now? Which are the lines that confirm the 170 azimuth? Was that the question? Is that what I'm supposed to show you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Just -- sorry. We'll get there. Follow my instructions carefully and one at a time. So you have drawn now a dotted line that depicts 220. Just put 220 on top of that dotted line for the moment.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, in the previous photograph you drew a horizontal line which you marked as C which allowed you to determine the direction as 170. If the direction was 220 degrees, where would that horizontal line be drawn? And I want you to draw it, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: [Marks]. Or, rather, it should be up here. Because we should expect to see the marks of the angle itself. And now I'll erase these. So this is where the line should be showing the marks. Again, just for the sake of a rough analogy, I will mention the blades of a helicopter. If it leaned one way, it would hit the ground. And that's the line we should be looking for. For example, this broken line, the line marked as G, but these marks are not there. I can't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That is what I want to ask you now. The marks that you talk about -- well, you've actually answered it, but again, to be clear, in this photograph, are there marks there that -- that would enable you and other experts to draw that horizontal line as you have drawn it now? Do you see those marks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: For the line marked as G to have a foundation for being drawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That's right. Are those marks there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: That's right. The line marked as G doesn't show any of the typical traces, horizontal ones, spreading from the centre of the explosion, and they should display a gentle curve of these prints on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And where do you see on this photograph again the typical traces, the typical horizontal traces spreading from the centre of the explosion? I want you to mark now -- I want to mark the last thing that you have drawn. Perhaps you can mark it as maybe -- M, did you say M?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mark it HM, as in horizontal marks.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P251, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Could I ask the court deputy to bring up 65 ter 891, and I'm interested in pages -- in the B/C/S, 22 to 30, and on the English version, the pages are 15 to 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness 137, on the right-hand side of your screen, do you see a document in your language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And what is that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: This is a typical document studying a certain incident, no matter what kind of incident. First it addresses the reason and the request that reached us for an analysis to be conducted. We were the bomb squad unit attached to the ministry and we covered the entire territory that we were in charge of, not just Sarajevo, and in full compliance with the hierarchy. The Sarajevo bomb squad, or rather, the CSB as can you see in the header, asked us to conduct an analysis. Of course they did, too, but officially they requested us to compile a report of our own.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And this report, does it relate to the Markale II incident? Can you see that there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If we could go to page 4. And could we arrange that that page is not broadcast since it has the witness's name on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, do you see your name there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The B/C/S version seems to have -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And on this page, do you see the determination of the direction of fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes. There's an azimuth of 170 degrees plus/minus 5 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to tender this document, that is pages 1 to 4 of this ter number into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P252 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, sticking to the same 65 ter number, can we go to page -- I think it's page 22. Sorry, page 29 of the B/C/S version. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, do you see a diagram there on the screen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you produce this diagram?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Could you very briefly explain what this diagram shows.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: After establishing the descent angle, based on the marks on the ground that we calculated to be 70 degrees, we measured the distance of the shell impact from the building and the height of the building. This diagram shows theoretically, the least possible angle under which the shell could have come. And based on these dimensions here, through very simple trigonometry, you can reach a conclusion that this degree could not have been less than 67 degrees, because otherwise, as you -- Their Honours asked me earlier in my evidence, this shell would have hit the roof of the building because that is a contact-fuse shell, it would have exploded there. So the possible descent angle, theoretically, is 67 or more. And independently of this diagram, we calculated the angle to be 70 degrees. We wanted to double-check this, that's why we remained there for a longer time measuring the distances from the building and by putting in these triangles as the basis for our calculation in order to prove that we were -- that we were correct and to rule out all other angles less than 60 or -- 70 degrees that were impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I just want to make a clarification. I heard on the interpretation that it was less -- you said less than 60 or 70 degrees. Do you mean less than 67 degrees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: I meant less than 67, because the geometry of this area, the building, the pavement indicates that this angle was impossible if it was less than 67. It is possible to be 67 or more, but in case of a smaller angle, under 67 degrees, the shell would have landed on the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
