utterances.text: Now you see the figure there of 480. Do you see that figure there, 480?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And what does that signify?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: 460 is the distance from the place where the shell landed and was activated to the building itself, the edge of the building. And that's the basis for this geometrical calculation. To draw the angle that you see on the left, we just transposed this length as one part of the angle, the height was the other hand of the angle and then you have Alpha degree and that is on what our calculation was based.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, we'll move to a diagram that should assist you there. But I just want to confirm, when you say the place where the shell landed, do you mean the centre of the explosion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: I mean the place where the fuse contacted the ground and I'm referring also to the axis. The centre of explosion is the centre of the mass of the explosive charge of the shell. If you wish me to show you, I can do that with the red marker, even here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: No, we'll get to another diagram for the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For clarification, can we have the page range you wish to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: There's no range, it's just this page, which would be page 29.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be admitted as Exhibit P253, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And can we move now to page 30, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Okay, Witness 137, do you see a diagram on your screen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And what does this -- yeah, what does this diagram signify?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: This diagram illustrates the principle of how the descent angle is calculated. We made this drawing in Corel, and by entering data that we gathered on the spot, it should have provide the descent angle by a calculation. The centre of the explosion that you asked me a while ago is this circle in the centre of the shell and that's the explosion centre and the place of impact is the place where the fuse hit the ground and activated the shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can you please mark that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: [Marks]. What I marked here is the centre of explosion. The charge in the shell has its centre of mass. Since the charge is activated by a hydro-dynamic wave all through -- round. So it's not like when you light a fuse or a cigarette. But a high dynamic wave is sent from the fuse, which is here. The whole mass of the charge is activated at once. Where the mass is most dense, geometrically speaking, is where the centre of the explosion is and I marked it with this red dot. To the right and left of the centre of explosion, most shrapnel spread and that's where the most impact power of the shell is. What I'm marking here, red, is actually the line in a vertical cross-section where you can find the deepest traces of shrapnel and that is how they are recognisable, not only by the width but by the biggest depth. Of course, there are traces here as well, what I'm adding here now in the drawing. But this recognisable line is there showing the strongest impact from the explosion because it spreads by -- in terms of kinetic energy of shrapnel in these two directions that I marked with these two arrows. Hence, there's this analogy that I keep repeating with the helicopter blades. However, there are other directions, but their power is not so big and there's fewer shrapnel that spread if these directions. So if we approximate all this, the strongest impact on the -- the biggest trace that is left in the ground is shown here by this line and that is this elliptical shape that I drew in the previous photograph. And that's a very typical occurrence for this type of shell. So this is the place of impact, the centre of explosion is here, and the most marked traces are in the direction of these two arrows to the left and to the right. This is where the kinetic energy is stronger and this is where there's most shrapnel and they kill most people there. That's how they are distributed in the space and they leave the deepest trace apart from the place where the direct hit by the shell was made. This is a common known geometry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness 137, on what basis do you say that the dot you marked with C is the centre of the explosion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: The explosive charge in the shell explodes. The strongest impact is in the centre of its mass. And it's marked with C. That's the point of gravity both geometrical and physical of the charge, explosive charge. So from this point C, spreading into the area around, is when actually the explosion happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And can you mark with the letter F where the fuse goes into the ground on this diagram.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: [Marks]. That's the tip of the shell marked with the red dot here and the letter F.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P254, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness 137, I just want to ask you, when you went to the scene on that day, did you -- were you able to see the fuse in the ground when you went there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: The tip of the shell is actually its fuse. It was not the subject of our investigation because it was an irrelevant element. The stabiliser at the other end of the shell was important and I don't remember us finding this fuse, because it was not relevant for any further investigations; therefore, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Given the ground that this shell exploded on, in your experience, would the fuse have been intact or would it have been disfigured, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Since this was a very hard surface, the detonation blast of the shell disfigured it, flattened it, and it flew somewhere. I don't remember that we found it. But as I said, at that point in time, it was irrelevant for our investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can I now bring up, again from 65 ter 891, pages 6 to 16. Actually, sorry, 6 to 10. And perhaps this should not be broadcast either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Okay, Witness 137, let's try and move quickly here. Do you see a document there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And do you see your name on that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: What is this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: This is an official report compiled by the security services centre of the ministry. It contains the names of all those participating in the investigation of this specific event.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender this document; that is, pages 6 to 10 into evidence, under seal, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P255, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness 137, do you recall investigating an incident in Dobrinja at Mustafa Kamanica Street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: If you're referring to the line for water inside the school yard where the pump was, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you recall when that was, roughly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: I think it was spring or summer. It was warm anyway. I have difficulties with establishing dates because there was so many events condensed and we were unable to remember the dates but we just remember the effects of these incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: With respect to this incident, did you perform an on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: If you're referring to the queue for water inside the school yard in Dobrinja, yes. We investigated it in detail because it was an extremely tragic event.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Just explain very briefly with respect to this incident in Dobrinja, what did you find when you got to the scene?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: We found huge pools of blood. It was a kind of concealed water pump because most of the time Sarajevo was without water because that was a sort of blackmail and people came with jerrycans to whatever pumps they could find to get the water and take it home. There was the pump inside the school yard that -- and it was in the area that didn't have a roof. It was an open area in the school possibly the size of half of this room where we are size now. The shell hit the window of the gym and luckily if it had been activated 10 centimetre to the other side, it would have come directly through the window. It was activated 10 centimetres above peoples' heads and there were many, many dead people and people injured in their upper bodies because the shrapnel rain virtually fell on the people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: What kind of school was this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: That was an elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Was the water pump used by civilians or by the military?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Look, everybody needs water. Everybody needs water and it's impossible to live without it. Since groundwaters in this area are very close, you just need to stick a pipe into the ground one or two metres and then you can use a mechanical pump to pump it out. As far as I remember in this particular incident, all of the people who were killed were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in your investigation, did you find any evidence of military facilities or military persons in the vicinity of this incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: This school at the very outset of the war was completely burned and destroyed. It had no furniture, no windows or doors, and it was rendered useless, other than a sort of shelter where people installed a pump where people can wait for a long time in a queue in safety to get their water and to take it home. There were no military facilities around or any military strongholds built near the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Upon your investigation, did you produce a report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We determined which explosive was used, from which direction it had come. The descent angle was not possible to establish because it hit the very edge of the window of the gym. So we didn't have the same situation as we had previously with the asphalt, but based on the dark stains and the marks left, we were able to establish the exact azimuth and the direction from which the shell came.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to bring up 65 ter 0018, and I'm interested in -- no, actually, that's fine. And if it could not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness 137, do you see a document there on the screen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And is that a report related to the incident at the water pump?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, that's the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you see your name on that page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: In your investigation, did you determine the type of weapon that was used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes. We concluded that based on the stabiliser or the tail of the shell which was found on the spot, it was the same shell that had been fired at Markale II, contact fuse 120-millimetre mortar shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Is the direction or the azimuth stated in this report that you produced?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, we determined the azimuth and direction pointed directly from that location to Nedzarici that was in the hand of the occupation forces, so north-westerly from the place of impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you say occupation force, which army are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: I'm talking about the Bosnian Serb army. And I'm using this term because a long time before this shell fell, our flag was hoisted in New York representing an internationally-recognised, sovereign country.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, please, just answer the questions that I asked and if I need more information, I will extract that from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender this document into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is there an English translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, there is. There should be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There isn't an English translation in e-court, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Does this apply to the one that we admitted previously? Because if there is no translation, it will have to be marked for identification pending translation. But you say there is a translation, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. President. Because I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because we haven't seen the translation on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I don't know what has transpired in terms of being in e-court, but I understand it was detailed in the list of exhibits. In any event, I have the ERN - maybe that can assist - of the English translation. It's 00646548.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, that's still B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise. But in the spreadsheet that we sent to the Defence ant to the Court, I have indicated with ERN, the English translation, so I don't understand what has happened here. In any case, I have a hard copy if you'd like to...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. Can I ask you? We admitted, I think, one or two other documents like this, and I don't believe we had an English translation on the screen. So I'll ask the court deputy to check that and he doesn't have to give me the information now; we can deal with it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The way to deal with this, then, is we'll mark it for identification, pending production of the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked for identification as P256.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, do you want me to answer your question about the previous document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, if you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I understand that they have been translated and the images were shown on the screen, from what I can recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, if -- in that case, then, we need not worry about that. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Can we move to 65 ter 00119. These are photographs. Actually, the pages I want are pages 8 to 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I say at this stage that I hope we will finish with the witness today since I have received an indication that he would like to be able to travel as soon as possible. But I would like to assure Mr. Tapuskovic that I will not allow that to prejudice the time that he has for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I -- I have been attempting as much as possible to take this examination as swiftly as possible. I would, with respect, submit that some of the questions that Your Honours had asked required follow up questions on my part, and therefore it has not been as swift as I would have liked, but I'm endeavouring to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can we move to page 10 of this document, please, 65 ter 119.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, do you see photographs on your screen there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: What are those photographs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: In the upper photograph you can see that the school was totally destroyed and could no longer be used for anything at all. In the lower photograph you see this closed area, a hidden area, if you like, were there was a water pump. You can see it right in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And can we move to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, does this photograph -- or do these photographs show where the shell landed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And can you -- can you point that out, please, or mark it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: There's an arrow showing just that. A shell landed here. We found a fin of the shell behind this wall. Because there should be a window of the gym but it's not there, and the shell hit just the edge of that. And had the shell flown on for about 10 or 15 centimetres, it would ended up in the gym and nobody would have been injured. But it went off at an altitude of maybe about two and a half or three metres above the ground which the upper photograph shows. And can you see the water vessels. So that's where people were standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you earlier used the phrase "the shrapnel rained -- rained down." What is it about the way that the shell hit the wall that enabled the shrapnel to do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: This is the silhouette of the shell; that's what I've drawn. As seen previously in Markale 2, this is how the shrapnel spreads, statistically speaking in most cases. So if you look at the upper photograph, you look at the place it landed. You see that the distribution of the shrapnel was like this from an altitude and down on to the persons standing there. There were a great many injured persons, which only goes to show that it was shrapnel smashing their heads. Some people were missing half of their crania with brains spilling all over the place, just because the shell landed where it did. On account of the geometrical distribution of the shrapnel, this was precisely what happened. The shrapnel blew off peoples' heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Just in both photographs where you have drawn the shell hitting the wall, can you just put the letter S on top of them, or beside them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: [Marks]. I'm sorry. At this point in time, I must say that my signature now and the signature that you saw on these documents 13 years, me having used it for a long time, it's difficult, of course, but the signature that I confirmed on those documents is my signature. The simple fact is that after a very long time, my signature has changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps there was a problem with the translation. I don't remember asking you to put your signature. Actually, so we don't confuse the photographs, can you erase your signature, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender these two photographs into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P257, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, these photographs are part of a range of photographs, and I'd like to have this range of photographs admitted, and I submit that it would not be in the interests of time to go through each and every page. But the witness has already given evidence that these photographs relate to the incident that he investigated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the range of photographs?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The range is 65 ter 00119 and it's pages 10 to -- I think it's 10 to 19 or 10 to 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One thing we didn't hear was when these photographs were taken, just to avoid returning to it. When were the photographs taken?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you answer that, Witness? When were the photographs taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't take them myself. I just saw the photographs. Can they please be shown again and then I will be able to tell you whether they were taken on the spot or in the morgue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, these photographs which the Prosecutor has just tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe the witness was answering the question in relation to these two photographs, and he has asked to be shown the other photographs and then he would be in a better position to say when these two were taken. Am I right, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us see the other. And that would represent the range of photographs that you are seeking to have admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It's just that it was -- I can go one by one. It would take time. And also, they do show images that are not -- just not pleasant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, the question raised by Mr. Tapuskovic is an important one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Perhaps we can go to the first page, which is, I understand, page 10 of this range. The page before that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, do you see a date there that says when these photographs were taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: It's quite illegible. It looks like the 10th of June, 1995. It's a bit clearer now. The 10th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is it the 10th or the 18th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, once it has been zoomed in, this might be an 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Next one. Well, would that be -- would that be true then? Would that help him? Do you wish to see the others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the question was, where were the photographs taken?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not where, when. The question is when, not where.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know because I wasn't the one who took them, nor were any of my colleagues. So I think it was done by the security services centre of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, Witness 137, can I just ask you this, then, do these photographs appear -- does this photo documentation appear to you to be authentic records from the Sarajevo police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And do these photographs relate to the incident in Dobrinja that you investigated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And on the first page of these photographs, did you see the date there, 18th of June, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: I must say that I couldn't distinguish if that was a 0 or an 8 and I don't think anybody could tell with certainty based on this photocopy. I had nothing to do with the making of these photographs. Therefore, I can hardly say when they were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes. And you did say, in fact, in your answer: "Yes, once this has been zoomed in, this might be an 8." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes I do remember that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, I don't think you can take it any further without cross-examining your own witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. I would still ask that these photographs are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're now speaking about the range.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P258, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can we move to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How much longer do you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: At the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It looks very doubtful as to whether the witness will be able to leave today, unless the cross-examination will take less than a session. It's time for the break, so we'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Before I move on, I just would like to inform the Court that the translation for MFI P256 is now, I understand, uploaded and therefore I would like to tender the document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can the court deputy bring up 65 ter 00113. And before I -- with respect to the last document, I would ask that it's admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just to be sure, that was 65 ter 00119, pages 10 through 19. Admitted as Exhibit P258. That will be admitted under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Prosecutor has confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes. Excuse me. Firstly, am I understanding correctly that the image is not being broadcast? Thank you, Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, do you see a document there on your screen, in your language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And what is this document, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: This is a typical official report on an incident like this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And do you see your name there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Does this document relate to the incident that you investigated in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, the Simone Bolivar elementary school. Yes, that is the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And does this document appear to you to be an authentic report from the Sarajevo police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that this document be tendered under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As Exhibit P259, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, did you also, in addition to mortars, undertake investigations of modified air bombs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And your role in the investigation of modified air bombs, would it be the same as that with respect to mortar incidents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: More frequently than not, our task was to collect the pieces found at a site and to identify what this was. I was a member of a team several times, teams set up to investigate incidents like these.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Were there times that you were involved in an investigation but did not actually go to the site?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, that is precisely what I said. We would be given components. We were supposed to analyse those and decide where they came from. They were normally component parts of rocket motors. Within a month, sometimes a room as big as this courtroom would be filled up with these. That's how many kept coming in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you recall conducting an investigation in respect of an incident at Savica Zajika Street, number 43.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Could I please see the document. As far as I remember, this is near the TV building, but I'm not certain. If I get to see the document, I'm sure that I can authenticate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If the Court Deputy can be bring up 65 ter 00013, and I'm interested in pages 22 to 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, do you see a document on the screen in your language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And what does it relate to, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: I think this is about a modified air bomb, given the fact that the pipes that were brought in, submitted for analysis, are somewhat big, and the pieces of tin. That's what usually can be found at the site of an explosion of a modified air bomb. You describe these parts and you try to ascertain where the parts came from. In this particular case, I think we were dealing with a modified air bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can we move to page 24, please. And I understand it's still not being broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That has been confirmed by the court deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, do you see your initials on this page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can I take it, then, that you produced this report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: I can't be certain why my initials are there and not my signature. But the report strikes me as absolutely authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you see the name there, Mirsad Jamakovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And who was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: He is the head of the bomb squad department, or was, for as long as I was a member of that unit, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And on this page, is it indicated that the weapon was a modified air bomb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Based on the description of the parts, that seems to be the case. These are rocket motors referred to as Grad, G-r-a-d. There was a huge stockpile of these and they couldn't be used in any other way, except for this way, unfortunately. These were meant to be used for plane travel and now they were used for these bombs. They were -- rockets were launched that were not a standard weapon in any army in the world. But if you modified this and you add very powerful rocket motors, you can make a very powerful weapon that can wreak a lot of destruction, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In this case, did you go to the site?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please look at page 1 where there is a description of a possible on-site investigation. Or was, perhaps, this analysis conducted based on any component parts that were eventually submitted, the page -- the first page, thank you. It says quite clearly that we received from the Sarajevo security services centre material that was submitted to us for analysis, and there's a list of components that were submitted. It was based on these parts that were supposed to produce a report, an expert report. By looking at this, I can conclude that we analysed the parts that were submitted to us for expert analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So the answer is that you did not go to the site for this one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's what I can tell, based on the document. I would like to remind the Chamber that it has been a very long time and I have not since refreshed my memory in any way, not even before I appeared before the Court. All I rely on is my memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Apart from the physical material that would have been sent to you by the Sarajevo security services, what else would you have received from them on the basis of which you would have carried out your analysis and come to a conclusion? In fact, I will just put it more bluntly: Did you receive a written report from them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would receive these components, these parts, for analysis as well as a request, a document listing the pieces that are being sent to us and telling us exactly what sort of analysis we're supposed to carry out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But somebody from the security services who was on site would have had do some basic work, such as measurements and so on. So what I wanted to find out from you was whether you would have received a written report from the security services with that kind of information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Depending on the case, when they, picked up the pieces, they would provide the description of the scene and provide all the measurements that could be of interest for the investigation and their comments. So in this brief request, they would just give a short description of the event, the most important elements thereof, and specify the pieces sent to us requesting us to analyse it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would any of the persons in the security services carrying out that basic investigation have had the kind of qualifications and training that you have had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to my experience, the analysis that they carried out were very fair, and they restricted themselves to the conclusions up to the level that they were able to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's not the question I asked. I asked whether any of the persons who were on the scene and who would have to had to carry out what I would call very basic investigations, taking measurements, taking photographs, whether any of those persons would have had the kind of qualifications and training that you had.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] More or less, yes. These were our regular briefings in which we conveyed to people our experience. It was teamwork in the broader sense of the meaning, both in terms of the KDZ and the Sarajevo security services centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because I'm particularly concerned to ascertain whether they would know what to look for in the way that you would know what to look for, based on your qualifications and experience.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that they knew exactly what to look for, that they assessed all the necessary elements professionally, the elements that were required for investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can we just go back to page 24 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness 137, do you see there on that document where it is written "FAB, 250 M72"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And can you explain to the Court what that means.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: It's an abbreviation of "few gas aerial bomb." 250 indicates its mass and M72 is its specification mark. These were bombs intended to be dropped from an aeroplane, heavy weight. This mass, 250, I think, is in kilograms, and half of this mass is actually explosive.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender this document under seal, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P260, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness 137, just a last few questions now. You told us earlier on in your evidence that prior to joining the police you worked for the Bosnian army deactivating unexploded weapons. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Given your knowledge from that role in the ABiH and your work with the police thereafter, can you answer the question as to whether the Bosnian government forces possessed modified air bombs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: I'm personally absolutely convinced that they didn't. They didn't have those type of bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you say why are you convinced that the ABiH didn't have modified air bombs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because the Yugoslav People's Army had all weapons depots under their control. Secondly, the Territorial Defence, organised locally, was practically disarmed before the war, and by its nature it didn't have in their depots these type of bombs. Since all the weapons were practically taken by the JNA, and the huge majority of that quantity was handed over to the Bosnian Serb army, it was practically impossible for us to get hold of these kinds of weapons, especially these kinds of bombs that would have been useless to us. And in those terms it means that we simply didn't have them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure that it really explains to me why they wouldn't have the weapons, but perhaps Mr. Tapuskovic may wish to take that matter up with you further. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sorry, may I just ask one question from the witness's previous answer before I conclude?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: A second bite at the cherry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Actually not. I just want to explain something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness 137, you said, "These kinds of bombs would have been useless to us." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: What I mean is that as such we could not have used them or launched them because we didn't have those rocket engines that were used to manufacture these devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That is the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I probably did not intend to begin with this issue that has just been raised, but in order not to forget it, I would like first to tackle that specific topic. Mr. Witness, I am a Defence counsel of Mr. Milosevic. My name is Tapuskovic, an attorney-at-law from Belgrade. And I will try to ask you, as directly as possible, about the things that you mentioned in your replies to the Prosecutor. Speaking of this particular subject, i.e., the weapon that only the Bosnian Serb army had, on the 15th of February, that is, a few days ago, you told Mr. Sachdeva and it read as follows: The witness said that the KDZ police unit of which he was a member was not part of the army. They didn't go to the front line; they didn't drive tanks; they didn't wear military uniforms. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But before you became a member of this special police unit, you had been in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and you were in uniform.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What were you wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: I was wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that my microphone is switching on by itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that you did civilian work for the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Quite simply, we didn't have uniforms. We were not only disarmed, but we didn't have any uniforms at all.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, excuse the interruption. The reason counsel's microphone is being shut on and off is because it is being controlled from the AV booth, because it's essential to have the microphone shut off when the witness is speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because he is protected.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you say that until 1994, the BH army practically had no weapons; that the area where you operated as part of the BH army was completely demilitarised.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any weapons in Sarajevo with the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: There were -- there were weapons that were totally ill-matched for the force that we were exposed to. It consisted mostly of small weapons and mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you allege that the BH army throughout the whole war, both while you were a policeman and otherwise, never had any weapons.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the army. I'm talking about the periods --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's not what he is alleging. He actually answered the question and said the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had -- I think the witness mentioned mortars and small arms, which does not mean "had no weapons."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that is so, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will have to use something that I never uttered before. I'm going to ask you directly --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that they had heavy weapons including tanks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: On various occasions we seized guns in depth of the Bosnian territory and on Mount Igman and that is how we got hold of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any cases that you transported them in pieces like Howitzers through the tunnel that existed there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: While I was a member of the army and later on the police, I have no experience of that nature or any knowledge of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever pass through the tunnel under the Butmir airport?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll get back to that later. You said in this information: "However, part of my assignment was to investigate the scenes and that he and his colleagues disarmed the shells that did not explode and subsequently they would hand them over to the army." My question is, those bombs or shells that you handed over to the army, did you do that in order for the army to use them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Of course. What else was the army to do but use explosives that they cannot get hold of any other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then these bombs were depicted as something manufactured in Krusik factory in Valjevo; was that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: No, no, it's not true at all. The projectiles that fell but did not explode were subsequently totally unusable and unlaunchable. By risking our lives, we disarmed these bombs in order for our army to get at least some crumbs of explosive that would be used for defence to which every living creature is entitled.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that, but what you want to say is, that at the time when the conflict broke out in Sarajevo between the warring parties, you say between the aggressor - it's fine with me, I respect your attitude - that the BH army in Sarajevo itself did not have enough weapons that had originally belonged to the Yugoslavia People's Army. And not only Sarajevo, that was the case throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina. That means that they had the same weapons, maybe not the same exactly like the Serbian army, but they had weapons that had belonged to the Yugoslav People's Army from the very outset of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: The difference between the type of weapons is so huge that one can say that the BH army was practically formed by the Territorial Defence as was actually non-existent. It was Territorial Defence, civilians, and police. The latter give the most contribution at the beginning of the war because they were the only organised force capable of putting up resistance and defence which means that we entered this war totally unprepared and unarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You know nothing about 200.000 armed paramilitaries that were there in January 1992 according to documents that have been written about nowadays by very representable members of your army. That in the beginning of 1992, there were 200.000 armed paramilitary. You know nothing about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: I know nothing about that, but the country that has its flag in New York and that has been recognised as an independent country cannot possibly have any paramilitary forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will try to be as efficient as possible and I don't know where to begin in the whole plethora of these matters. But let me, Mr. Witness, start with this particular incident. But let us clarify this incident before the Chamber, who are going to rule on this. Everything that happened in the school that had been destroyed, the school called Simone Bolivar, on the 18th of June, 1995. If I understood you correctly, you just said that these people, seven of them were killed, a large number were wounded, that they were -- became victims in a kind of shelter and that is where they were hit. Some of them lost their lives, some sustained serious injuries as described in your report. So you say that they were in a shelter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes. That is not a standard shelter. That is a confined area within the school that had glass roof which was then broken. So it was a kind of secluded area within the school which had an open roof, but you may call it a shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But the people who were in this shelter could not have been seen by anyone, anyone looking from the outside. And this was all in Dobrinja, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is the Dobrinja neighbourhood the part of Sarajevo that was partly under the control of the BH army and partly under the control of the army of Republika Srpska. Is it fair to say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that this school was approximately four or 500 metres from the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Approximately, roughly speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown document DD00-871. Page 1 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you see this document in front of you? Is that a dispatch as it says here at the top?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the contents. I will not dwell long about it. It speaks about the 18th of June. It talks about the victims, the casualties --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, where is the English translation of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, -- Your Honours, I received this document from the Prosecution. It has its number. I don't have the translation. I have the Prosecution number, and that's the document I received from them. And if it's of any significance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... your responsibility or some member of your team to ensure that there is a translation. Is there a translation, Mr. Sachdeva?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that can be checked. But I just want to clarify that this is not a document that I had put on my list 48 hours prior to the evidence of this witness. It may have been disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. And Mr. Tapuskovic, you must appreciate that receiving a document from the Prosecution doesn't relieve you of the duty to ensure that it is in order for presentation in court. Well, there is no translation available here. Let us see whether we can proceed on the basis of the interpretation we'll receive.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I made a great effort together with my team to check whether there is a translation available. However, the only thing I am seeking from this document is for the interpreters to say to witness that this dispatch refers to the 18th of June and that it contains the names of the victims. I would like the witness to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: I don't see who sent this dispatch and to whom. Therefore, in order to analyse it or confirm any content thereof, I would require more data. It says "MUP RBIH" and it says also "CSB Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The security service, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: The security services centre of Sarajevo. That's practically the Sarajevo police.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I will not dwell on this longer and I do not seek this document to be tendered at all. I just wanted everyone to know that this dispatch exists. However, there's another document, DD00-0872. Can we first go into private session for me to -- private or closed session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not going through all of this now. I'm not reading it out. Some of it has been discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Here, for example, in paragraph 2, you say there was a lot of blood around the pump as well as bits of tissue, brains, bones, crania, pools of blood. Is that what paragraph 2 says?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: I can't see it right now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 2 on that page.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Two paragraphs down. "All the traces found were fixed and photographed. Pieces of shrapnel and a projectile stabiliser were submitted for analysis."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: A while ago, in answer to one of the Prosecutor's questions, you said what you said about finding the fins, the tail-end of the shell, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And that assisted you greatly, although it bounced backwards in establishing the direction from which the shell came?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: That's not what I said. The tail was found in a room where there were no victims. The shell hit the edge of the window, and then the tail just continued and eventually landed in the gym. But in order to determine the direction, you don't use, in this case, the tail. You use the marks of the explosive that were clearly visible on the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about when a shell impacts against a hard solid surface? Where does the tail usually go? What happens to it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: That depends on how hard a surface is. When there is a explosion, this creates a huge vacuum and the tail is often sucked into the ground or tarmac, such as was the case in Markale I. The tail drilled into the ground. After some cleaning, a member of UNPROFOR found it and extracted it. Here this was not the case because the shell did not impact against the vertical or horizontal surface. It landed on the edge of a wall, exploded right there and the shrapnel rained down on the persons standing below.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned this tail in connection with the Simone Bolivar school. That's why I'm asking. Where at Markale was the tail of that shell found, the shell that exploded there. Was in the hole that we looked at a while ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: No, it wasn't, it wasn't in the hole. Unlike Markale I, it bounced some distance from the place itself. The surface, the ground is very hard, and the depression it created was very small. And this shell was made to -- was built in a way as to explode instantaneously. It does not have a delayed explosion such as many other projectiles do. It wasn't built that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, in the case of Markale II, the 28th of August, the tail of the projectile was not found like it normally is because of what you say, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: No, it's not like that. We can't call anything normal here. It depends on how hard a surface is. Sometimes it sucks the tail in, such as in the case of Markale I. If it's a particularly hard surface, the tail ricochets, bounces to the left or to the right, carried by the force of the detonation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us now move on to the last page of this document. Can you please confirm who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies to the Prosecutor. I don't know if the signatory of this document is perhaps a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is this witness protected? I'm asking the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, he is protected.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have asked the audiovisual booth not to broadcast this document, so we should be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could keep the document on our screens but without the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you look, please, at the second-last paragraph, just before the list. It reads: "At the Dobrinja hospital, while the files on those killed and wounded were being compiled, the UNMO observers arrived; Major Haga from Ireland and Captain Hansen from Denmark, as well as Major Abdulah from Jordan. All of them from the airport sector. They informed the on-site investigation team that they had been to the site and established the same fact as our own team." Is that true, is that what it reads, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it reads.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The very last paragraph is important to note that the general sector where citizens were harmed there are no firing positions of the BH army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about a radius of 500 metres, a distance of 500 metres? Would that still be within the area affected by military operations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Dobrinja was densely populated. It was like an ant hive; it was teeming with people. The school building itself was not a particularly interesting military target because it is much lower than the remaining buildings that surround it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, DD00-0872, can that, please, be admitted as a Defence exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's already in evidence as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document is DD00-0882. This is a mistake made by someone who was originally on the witness list, Thomas Hansen. Someone that we have mentioned already. He was dropped from the witness list. He gives this testimony. There is an English translation, and I would like to show the witness a portion of this statement. Page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The paragraph begins like this. "I think we finally..." It's down the middle of the page, halfway down. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: I would like to have that zoomed in. Yes, I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is what it says?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, now I can see it clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "I think we finally arrived on the scene about one to one and a half hours after the impact of the shell. At the time we arrived, the Bosnian Serb police had already carried out their investigation and had left." Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear counsel.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: The only thing we could see at the scene was a hole on the west wall, west side of the wall about four metres above the ground, some blood marks, bits of brain matter, and body parties." Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: By seeing the impact, in my opinion the shell came from the west and possibly from the north-west.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: I see that too but that is entirely incompetence. It is far too unspecific.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The next paragraph. "The Bosnian police had already removed the tail of the shell and the victims were taken to the Dobrinja hospital. Therefore, we were unable to conduct a proper investigation. The way the shell hit the wall it was obvious that the shell had been fired from a more or less westerly direction."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says. But my opinion is this report is inaccurate and incompetent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If the projectile had been fired from the west it would have been from the BH army positions, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: No. Because this says that they couldn't carry out a proper investigation. What's a proper investigation? Do we always have to wait for them to arrive on the scene, when in fact very often they don't show up at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Two paragraphs down the page. "We didn't see the bodies there, but since there were remains of human bodies found at the scene, a number of persons must have been killed." Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says. That's what the document says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please. Paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "Of course it was impossible to establish whether the tail of the shell was found at the exact -- at the same place where the shell had landed, but there was no reason for --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear this part of counsel's quote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the rest of your sentence following on from what you said "but there was no reason for". For what?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to avoid any misunderstanding, I have to read both paragraphs in their entirety, the first two paragraphs. "At the hospital, a Bosnian official showed me the tail of the shell which he claimed to have found at the scene. This was definitely the tail-fin of a 120-millimetre shell. Of course it was impossible for me to find out if this tail-fin had been found at the site of the incident but there was no reason for him to lie to me about this." Is that what says.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says. But that means absolutely nothing to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Two paragraphs further down the page. "When you see the confrontation line, west and north-west, from the point of impact, it is almost impossible to determine whether the shell was fired by BH mortar or a BSA mortar on account of the possible range of a 120-millimetre shell, it could have been fired from any of the sides." Is what it says?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: DD00-0882. I tender this into evidence as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D72, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just let me ascertain something, Mr. Tapuskovic. What was the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was on the 8th of September, 1995, as early as 1995, with the clashes still going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And it was an investigation into what incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Simone Bolivar school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to be clear, this document is not an investigation report or -- or conclusions of an investigation. It is a statement given to an ICTY investigator. It's not -- it's not a report that we've seen in -- during this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this same witness testified about that shell hitting the TV building. He was a witness first and then he was dropped. Here he talks about that too. But my learned friend will be dealing with that in a couple of days and I don't want to place this in connection with this witness. However, speaking of documents, I have two UNPROFOR documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know whether this is appropriate, but if learned counsel is attempting to draw some connection between this person who gave a statement with respect to the TV incident, in connection between what he has said regarding the TV incident and what is contained in this document with respect to this incident, I submit that there should not be any connection drawn whether advertent or inadvertant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us move on. Let us make the best use of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am really only using my time for the most pertinent issues. Your Honours, I have two UNPROFOR documents in relation precisely to what this witness has been testifying. One is dated the 18th and the other the 19th of June, that same year. Those are two documents. I can begin if you like, but it will take me some time for me to deal with these. This is UNPROFOR Sarajevo report the 18th of June 1995, 65 ter 532, 00532. At page 12 of that document -- and I could read that. I have translated this. I don't have the B/C/S, but can I read that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In this UNPROFOR report at page 12 -- there. We have it now. It says here, there's this list of Dobrinja incidents and then it reads at page 12: "UNMO team SW 2 carried out investigation of 120-millimetre MOR, origin, approx 320 MAG, difficult to confirm, fragments, removed by local civpol. Difficult to confirm because fragments found at the site had been removed by the local police. Damage could be seen on the concrete wall four metres above ground level. The impact occurred at a water collection point. UNMOs were allowed to visit Kosevo Hospital and the morgue where they could confirm seven civilians killed. They were informed that there were 10 injured casualties. UNMOs have not been allowed to visit hospitals since the 15th of June and are still not allowed to do so, but in this case an exception was made." So, Witness, this report provides no opinion at all, simply because your own team had removed evidence that could still be found at the scene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to be clear, in the English version at least, the word "because" is not included at all. I don't see the word "because."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. It's not an unreasonable inference to draw. "Difficult to confirm, fragments removed by local civilian police" and I think counsel is entitled to put that to the witness and ask him for his comment on that. But after this, we have to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So, Witness, sir, based on this, we see that it is not true that UNPROFOR confirmed everything that you had established at the site?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137
utterances.text: I never said UNPROFOR confirmed what we had established at the site, but rather a report that was compiled by somebody else, not myself. Secondly, what UNPROFOR are claiming here, this is so unspecific that it merits no attention at all. The text says "I heard from another person that he claimed that the TV building had been targeted." I heard from somebody else this or that. And then this estimate that the shell arrived from the north or the north-west. It is so unspecific that it merits no attention. Please tell me what it means?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And then the witness unintelligibly reads from the original document on the scene. Is this the azimuth? Is this --
